explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The speaker says the opposite: "Though I have fallen, I will arise…" (Micah 7:8). So the fall is real, but it isn't the end of the story. I've been face-down in a pile of chocolate chips plenty of times, and I promise you the floor is not where you stay.

That's right, friend. The speaker says, "Though I have fallen, I will arise…" (Micah 7:8). The enemy is told not to gloat, because the fall isn't the last word. I think that's a pretty bold thing to say to somebody who is watching you sit in the dark.

Yes, friend. The speaker says, "…though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light" (Micah 7:8). Darkness is the hard part of the sentence, and light is where it lands. I know a little about sitting in the dark, and a line like that hits me right in the apron.

A shield is a good thing to have, but that's not the word here. The speaker says, "…though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light" (Micah 7:8). Notice how the word fits the darkness, because the two go together. You don't hand somebody a shield when the problem is that nobody can see.

Rock is a strong word, friend, and the Bible does use it for God in other places. Here, though, the speaker says, "…though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light" (Micah 7:8). Light is the answer that matches the dark. A rock in a dark room just gives you something to stub your toe on.

explanations.answer: Until the LORD argues the case
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The speaker says the rage must be endured "until He argues my case and executes justice for me" (Micah 7:9). The speaker isn't running the case alone. The LORD takes it up Himself, and I think that's a comfort.

The enemy is in the passage, but the enemy doesn't set the timer. The speaker says the rage lasts "until He argues my case and executes justice for me" (Micah 7:9). So it's the LORD who brings the change. The gloating gets answered later, in verse 10.

explanations.answer: Until every debt is paid back
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd go there, friend, since bills are on everybody's mind. But the verse doesn't mention paying anything back. It says "until He argues my case and executes justice for me" (Micah 7:9). The LORD is the one who steps in.

Yes, friend. The enemy "will see and will be covered with shame" (Micah 7:10). She's the one who asked, "Where is the LORD your God?" Then she gets to watch what happens. I think that question is going to feel a lot smaller to her then.

Glory sounds nice, but it isn't what covers her. The verse says she "will see and will be covered with shame" (Micah 7:10). She had asked, "Where is the LORD your God?" Shame is what comes after that question.

Close in feel, friend, and darkness did show up earlier in verse 8. But the speaker was the one sitting in darkness, not the enemy. For her, verse 10 says she "will see and will be covered with shame." The light was headed the speaker's way.

That's the one, friend. "The day for rebuilding your walls will come—the day for extending your boundary" (Micah 7:11). Walls going up and borders growing is a picture of things getting better. I've always liked a day where the work is building instead of cleaning up.

Not this time, friend. The verse says "The day for rebuilding your walls will come—the day for extending your boundary" (Micah 7:11). Nobody is walking away from anything. Someone who abandons a wall doesn't go on to extend the boundary.

I get why breaking comes to mind after all that trampling. But verse 11 says "The day for rebuilding your walls will come—the day for extending your boundary." It's a building day, not a breaking day. The word that goes with a bigger boundary is rebuilding.

explanations.answer: Because of what its people did
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. The earth becomes desolate "because of its inhabitants, as the fruit of their deeds" (Micah 7:13). That's a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly. The text ties the desolation to what the people did.

Rain is a fair guess, friend, since a dry land can look desolate. But the verse doesn't say a word about rain. It says the earth becomes desolate "because of its inhabitants, as the fruit of their deeds" (Micah 7:13).

explanations.answer: Because its walls were never built
explanations.explanation: Walls were in the last verse, so I see the connection. But verse 11 was about rebuilding them, and verse 13 gives a different reason. The earth becomes desolate "because of its inhabitants, as the fruit of their deeds" (Micah 7:13).

Yes, friend. "As in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show My wonders" (Micah 7:15). The passage is looking back to the exodus, when God brought Israel out of Egypt. It says the wonders will be shown again.

Laws came after Egypt in Israel's story, so I see why you reached for that one. But the verse doesn't say laws. It says, "As in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show My wonders" (Micah 7:15).

Riches would be a nice thing to hear about, friend. But that's not what this verse promises. It says, "As in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show My wonders" (Micah 7:15). The word is wonders.

That's right, friend. Verse 17 says, "They will come trembling from their strongholds in the presence of the LORD our God; they will tremble in fear of You." The strongholds were the places they felt safe, and now they come out of them shaking. That's a long way from where they started.

Not quite, friend. The same verse that has them licking the dust also says, "They will come trembling from their strongholds in the presence of the LORD our God; they will tremble in fear of You" (Micah 7:17). So both parts are in the text. The statement was true.

Yes, friend. God "does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in loving devotion" (Micah 7:18). The reason is right there in the verse. The text points to who God is, not to anything people did.

explanations.answer: His people finally earned His favor
explanations.explanation: That's a tempting answer, friend, because earning feels fair. But the verse gives a different reason. God "does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in loving devotion" (Micah 7:18). It isn't about people earning anything.

The passage says the opposite, friend. The same verse says God "pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression" (Micah 7:18), and the speaker already said, "I have sinned against Him" (Micah 7:9). Pardon only makes sense when there's something to pardon. God's anger ends "because He delights in loving devotion."

explanations.answer: Into the depths of the sea
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. "You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea" (Micah 7:19). Depths is a deep word, and it gives the picture of sins being put far down. I think that's a good place to leave them.
The wilderness is a good guess, since it shows up in other parts of the Bible. But not in this verse. Micah 7:19 says, "You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea."

That one sounds familiar, friend, like something from another place in Scripture. But in this verse the words are different. Micah 7:19 says, "You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea."
Not quite, friend. The passage says God will act "as You swore to our fathers from the days of old" (Micah 7:20). So it's tied to something promised long ago. Nothing there says it's new.

Right, friend. The message ends with God showing "faithfulness to Jacob and loving devotion to Abraham, as You swore to our fathers from the days of old" (Micah 7:20). Jacob and Abraham were Israel's forefathers. So it's a promise God made long ago, and it isn't something new.
